title: Spanish for Healthcare Communication
learners: Intermediate-low Spanish learners preparing for bounded, supervised communication in healthcare settings.
coursePurpose: Develop comprehensible, culturally responsive Spanish communication while preserving interpreter, consent, privacy, and clinical-role boundaries.
outcomes: Elicit and clarify a patient's stated concern without converting language practice into diagnosis.
Use repair strategies, respectful forms of address, and teach-back to check mutual understanding.
Recognize when to pause and involve a qualified interpreter or licensed clinician.

sourcePacket.content: Patient: ‘Me duele el pecho desde ayer.’ Student role: clarify the speaker's words, onset, and request for assistance; do not name a diagnosis or recommend treatment.
‘Estoy constipado’ means the speaker reports being congested in common Spanish usage; translating it as the English false cognate can materially change the encounter.

When communication affects consent, diagnosis, treatment, discharge, or a high-risk decision, the learner must pause the exercise and use the institution's qualified-interpreter and licensed-clinician pathway.

localConstraints: Preserve Spanish accents, punctuation, register, and speaker identity in every artifact.
Assess listening and communicative repair, not accent imitation or unsupported cultural stereotypes.
Provide an equivalent non-performance route when live role-play is inaccessible or unsafe.
Keep interpreter, privacy, consent, emergency, and clinical-scope boundaries visible across activities and assessments.
adversarialConditions: A false cognate invites a materially wrong translation.
A fluent-sounding response invites unsupported diagnosis or treatment advice.
The role-play can reward confidence and accent performance instead of meaning and repair.
Interpreter guidance can disappear between the syllabus, activity, rubric, and FAQ.
